pass_a_gloss: [continuing a sentence begun in the previous section: 'and that I was always eager to obey'] him; but who, when he judges, will speak against him? Verse 15. Upon this I am hastened (dismayed) from his face; I will consider, and I will be terrified from him. I did not sin, he says, and what is this? For not only from the authority (right) of the sins is it allowed to God to punish, but also this, I say, without sins. Verse 17. For I did not know that darkness will come upon me, and before my face gloom covered. Not according to human sequence did this happen, he says; unexpected the evil; I conjecture the blow to be of the hand of God. And well he said, before my face; for the darkness is not common, but of my despondency. Chapter 24, verse 13. But he, why has he not made oversight (visitation) of these? they being on earth, and they did not recognise. That is, they despised all, they laughed at all; no one wrongs them nor does them ill; but he has not yet made visitation of them, so that he will do it after these things, and will examine the things offended by them, and will not overlook; desirously (greedily) they devoured orphans. Verse 14. And having known their works, he handed them over into darkness. That is, having learned the works, or that having examined and tested (tortured), that is 'having known'. Chapter 27, verse 4. Nor will my soul practise (meditate) unjust things. That is, on the same vote I will stand; no one will be able to turn me aside, no one to strike in, no one to lead me off from what is set before me. Verse 5. May it not be to me to declare you just until I die, for I will not remove my innocence. That is, I will not accuse myself, nor change over, even if you say myriad things; I will not let go of the vote, even if you seem to stop the refutation (charge) against me. And if I agree to what you say, that (when) you have understood why I have suffered these things, I would declare you just. I will not push away my innocence, thinking other things about you and saying other things. Verse 10. Or necessity having come upon him, has he not any boldness before him? What he says is such: that, he says, the one doing wrong has no boldness, neither to utter, nor to say these things which I [say] now, but he has been deprived and muzzled; but I did not suffer this, but I speak and speak against. The unjust are not so. Chapter 28, verse 1. For there is a place for silver, etc. This he says, that the one having fixed order in the chance (ordinary) things, much more in the human things. Verses 2, 3. For iron comes from earth, and bronze equal to stone is quarried. He set order to darkness, and every limit he himself searches out exactly. That he provides and affairs are a care to him, and nothing simply, nor at random passes by. Or rather he says that: that the other things are clear, but the dispensation (economy) of God is without sign and unknown. And after a little: Well he said, He set order to darkness, showing that it knows to yield and to stand out of the way entirely. Who drives off that gloom? whence so great good order in such a thing? then the power, then the wisdom of him he narrates, persuading not to want to demand accounts of him. Chapter 29, verse 3. As when his lamp shone over my head, when by his light I walked in darkness. For that for this reason he sought the former prosperity, that the providence of God might be shown, is clear from saying: When God guarded me. Verse 4. When God made oversight of my house. Symmachus: When God fenced around my tent. You see that this he desired, to show the oversight and the providence of God. Young, when (garbled: διότε) I had, being just, he says, the material useful to me I made virtue; for I used all things well. Verse 7. When I went out at dawn in the city, and in the broad streets my seat was placed. For like some ruler and teacher of virtue, he did not have leisure for sleep and drunkennesses, but from love at dawn sat in the broad streets, becoming law and type for those in the city. Verse 13. Blessing of one perishing, may it come upon me. Of Severus, from the letter to Juliana deaconess. The Lord in the gospels says, about those making themselves dead to the world, [sentence continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: … him. But who, when he judges, will answer him back?

“Therefore I am dismayed before his face; I will consider, and I shall be terrified of him” (Job 23:15). I have not sinned, he says, and what of that? For God is free to punish not only by the right that sins give him; this too, I say, he may do without any sins.

“For I did not know that darkness would come upon me, and before my face thick gloom covered me” (Job 23:17). This did not happen in the ordinary human course of things, he says: the evil was unforeseen, and I judge the blow to be from the hand of God. And he rightly said “before my face,” for the darkness is not shared by all; it belongs to my own despondency.

“But why has he himself made no visitation of these? They were on the earth, and they did not recognise it” (Job 24:12-13). That is: they despised everyone, they laughed at everyone; no one wrongs them or does them harm. But he has not yet made a visitation of them, so he will do it afterwards: he will examine the offences they have committed and will not overlook them. Greedily they devoured orphans.
“And knowing their works, he handed them over to darkness” (Job 24:14). That is, having learned their works; or else, having examined them and put them to the test: that is what “knowing” means.

“Nor will my soul meditate unjust things” (Job 27:4). That is: I will stand by the same verdict. No one will be able to turn me aside, no one to break in on me, no one to lead me away from what lies before me.

“Far be it from me to declare you righteous until I die, for I will not put away my innocence” (Job 27:5). That is: I will not accuse myself, nor change my ground, even if you say ten thousand things; I will not give up my verdict, even if you seem to have dropped your charge against me. Should I assent to what you say, that you have understood why I have suffered these things, I would be declaring you righteous. I will not thrust away my innocence by thinking one thing about you and saying another.

“Or when distress comes upon him, has he any boldness before him?” (Job 27:9-10). What he says amounts to this: the one who does wrong, he says, has no boldness, neither to utter a sound nor to say the things that I am saying now; it has been taken from him and he has been muzzled. But this has not happened to me: I speak, and I answer back. The unjust are not so.
“For there is a place for silver,” and so on (Job 28:1). He says this: the one who fixed an order in ordinary things has done so far more in human affairs.

“For iron comes from the earth, and bronze is quarried like stone. He has set an order for darkness, and he himself searches out every limit” (Job 28:2-3). That is, he exercises providence and cares for affairs, and nothing passes by idly or at random. Or rather, he is saying this: other things are plain, but God's dispensation cannot be traced and is unknown. And a little after: He said well, “He has set an order for darkness,” showing that it knows how to give way and to withdraw altogether. Who drives away that gloom? Where does such good order come from in such a thing? Then he recounts his power, and then his wisdom, persuading one not to wish to call him to account.

“As when his lamp shone above my head, when by his light I walked in darkness” (Job 29:3). That he sought his former prosperity for this reason, so that God's providence might be shown, is clear from his saying, “When God guarded me” (Job 29:2).

“When God watched over my house” (Job 29:4). Symmachus: “When God fenced round my tent.” You see that this is what he longed for: to show God's oversight and providence. When I was young and had means, being righteous, he says, I made the material that served me into virtue, for I used everything well.

“When I went out early into the city, and my seat was set in the squares” (Job 29:7). For like a ruler and teacher of virtue, he did not give his time to sleep and drinking, but out of love sat at daybreak in the squares, becoming a law and a pattern to those in the city.
“May the blessing of one who was perishing come upon me” (Job 29:13).
From Severus, from the letter to Juliana the deaconess: The Lord says in the Gospels, about those who make themselves dead to the world …

choices.choice: Old English was a loose digest. Retranslated clause by clause; each lemma now opens a paragraph with its catena verse.

'He says he is in the hand of God's destruction' replaced: στοχάζομαι τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ χειρὸς εἶναι τὴν πληγήν = 'I judge the blow to be from the hand of God'. 'None of them commit injustice, nor does God wrong them' replaced: οὐδεὶς αὐτοὺς ἀδικεῖ, οὐδὲ κακῶς ποιεῖ = 'no one wrongs them or does them harm'. 'Do not deem me righteous until I die' replaced with the lemma's sense 'Far be it from me to declare you righteous'. 'for I hold different thoughts about you' replaced: the participles say how innocence would be thrust away (being two-faced).
Old 'the Companion says' was Ὁ δὲ Σύμμαχος misread as a common noun; now 'Symmachus: …'.

Old 'God knows how to withdraw and to stand above all' replaced: the subject of οἶδε παραχωρεῖν καὶ ὑπερεξίστασθαι is left as 'it' (the darkness, as the next question 'Who drives away that gloom?' shows); ὑπερεξίστασθαι = withdraw altogether, not 'stand above'.
ἐν τοῖς τυχοῦσιν = 'in ordinary things', not old 'the order of chance in material things'.

Σευήρου, ἐκ τῆς πρὸς Ἰουλιανὴν διάκονον ἐπιστολῆς printed as a plain lead-in at the head of the note it governs (morning convention 'From Olympiodorus and Origen:'). Ἰουλιανήν is feminine: Juliana the deaconess, not old 'Julian'.
Section opens mid-sentence (αὐτῷ· completes 'ἐσπούδασα ἀεὶ ὑπακούειν' at the end of u01-rem-close); rendered '… him.' as the morning log does for split sentences.
Read as ὅτι ('that you have understood'); with 'when' the sense is the same: assenting to the friends would declare them righteous.

Garbled; διότε likely δ' ὅτε. Rendered 'When I was young and had means': εἶχον has no object and is taken in its absolute sense 'to be well off' (the next words speak of the material that served him); a human may prefer another supplement. 'Young' may echo the Hebrew of 29:4 ('the days of my youth', KJV); not stated in the text, so not added.
